source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (1924), tale 85 'Man-Snake as Bridegroom' (a, Richard Morgan; b, Matilda Hall)

summary.en: A pick-and-choose girl accepts a coal-black pretty man who eats nothing but raw eggs and borrows the whole wedding outfit. On the road he sheds the borrowed finery piece by piece, walks her into a cave, turns a yellow snake, and sings 'a handsome man will kill you' over her rescue-song until the neglected brother Collin — in the bush shooting birds — hears his name, shoots the snake-head at her nose, and saves a sister who never counted him before.
summary.zh: 挑挑剔剔的姑娘看中一位烏黑俊郎——只生吞生蛋、婚禮行頭全靠借。歸途他一路脫下借來的衣飾，把她帶進洞穴，化作黃蛇，邊唱『俊郎者殺你』邊聽她呼救；被冷落的弟弟科林在林中打鳥聞名趕至，一槍擊中抵近鼻尖的蛇頭，救下從前從不把他放在眼裡的姐姐。

sensitivity.note: Animal-bridegroom cycle (ATU 425-linked). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was a woman to court. Every man came to court her and she said she did not want him, until one day she saw a coal-black man, a pretty man. 'O mother, this is my courtier!' She took the man; at breakfast and dinner he did not eat, only sucked a couple of raw eggs. She had a brother named Collin whom she did not count. 'Sister, the man you are going to marry is a snake.' — 'Boy, you ever hear snake can turn man?' — 'All right! The day you are married, I will be in the bush shooting my bird.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 85a (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the wedding day, when the marrying was over, the man took his wife, all his wedding garments borrowed; going home, everywhere he went, all those things he borrowed he shed off one by one till at the last house he took off the last piece — the Bogie! He walked with his wife into the wood and to a cave, put her down to sit, turned a yellow snake, sat in his wife's lap with his head pointed to her nose to suck her blood and kill her. The woman sang, 'Collin now, Collin now, fe me li'l brudder callin' come o!' — and the Snake said, 'Urn hum, hum he; a handsome man you want, a handsome man will kill you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 85a, middle (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Collin said, 'Wonder who is singing my name in this middle wood?' and walked fast with his gun. When he came to the cave the snake's head was just going to touch the woman's nose; Collin shot him with the gun and took out his sister — and she never counted her brother till her brother saved her life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 85a, ending (1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the paired version the well-pleased parents marry the Yellow Snake to their daughter, and halfway home he drops trousers, shirt and jacket, goes into a hole, puts out his head, lays hold of his wife's leg and swallows to the hip — 'Worra worra, me wi' swallow yo', swallow yo' till yo' mamma can't find yo'!' — while the girl sings for her hunter-brothers, Harry, Tom and John, who hear her crying, kill the Snake, and take the sister away: 'Pick and choose isn't good; if you weren't pick and choose, you wouldn't have married the Yellow Snake that was going to kill you now.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 85a-2 'The Rescue (2)' (1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Girls Who Married the Devil

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (1924), tale 86a 'The Devil-husband' (told by William Forbes, Dry River)

summary.en: The despised yawzy little brother turns cockroach and rides in the boat when the Devil carries his sisters home. Warned by the house-maid — 'He is Devil!' — the maid sets them loose each day by throwing out bags of corn, rice and barley for the talkative cock, who sings 'Massa handsome wife gone!' as the girls catch the boat; the Devil returns stamping 'John Studee!' to turn the boat back — until the last bag empties just in time, and only the little cockroach-brother's cunning saves them from the Devil.
summary.zh: 遭嫌棄的癬病弟弟化作蟑螂藏入小船，隨魔鬼把兩位姐姐載回家。女僕警告『他是魔鬼！』，並每日傾出成袋玉米、大米與大麥喂那隻多話的公雞；雞唱『主人俊美的妻子走了！』姑娘們便得以登船；魔鬼聞聲跺腳喚船『約翰·斯圖迪！』——直到最後一袋見底，船才及時離岸；若非蟑螂弟弟的機巧，魔鬼早已把她們害了。

sensitivity.note: Devil-husband escape tale (ATU 311-linked). Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There were two sisters who had a yawzy brother whom the sisters did not care about; they were fatherless and motherless. A man came to court the two sisters to carry them away, took them into the boat to carry home, and the little yawzy boy turned a cockroach and got into the boat. When they got home the house-maid told the two girls, 'What you follow this man come here now for? He is Devil!' The Devil told the house-maid she must feed them well, and the little boy came out of the boat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 86a (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The house-maid said she would send them home in the boat, threw out a bag of corn for the big cock in the yard, saying that when he ate it done the boat would catch home. The cock commenced to eat — 'Hock kaluck kum ka turn swallow!' — knocking his wing bap-bap, then crowing, 'Ko ko re ko! Massa handsome wife gone!' Devil did not hear him; the cock crowed again and Devil heard now, and came singing 'Zin-ge-lay, wid dem run come, wid dem jump come, wid dem walk fas'!' The boat's name was John Studee; as he ran into the yard he stamped his foot and said 'John Studee!' — and the boat turned right back with the two girls and the little boy; as they most came, the little boy turned cockroach again and went in the garden, and the Devil didn't see him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 86a, middle (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning the Devil put the two girls up again; the maid threw out a bag of corn and a bag of rice — the same thing happened. The last day she threw out a bag of corn, a bag of rice and a bag of barley, and after the cock ate off the three bags, the time the girls caught home, leaving the boat at the shore-side, the cock clapped his wing — 'Plop plop! Massa handsome wife gone!' As the Devil heard, him came singing his song, stamped his foot and said 'John Studee-e!' — but the boat turned right back home; and if it wasn't for that little yawzy boy, the Devil would have killed them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 86a, ending (2024/1924); not verbatim.

title.en: The Snake-husband and His Borrowed Collars

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (2024), tale 86b 'The Snake-husband' (told by Emilina Dodd, Lacovia)

summary.en: On the drive home the finely dressed suitor must hand back collar, jacket and everything, one borrowed piece at a time, until he shows himself plain as a snake. He locks his bride up to kill her when he finds the 'bump'; the mother-in-law frees her with a barrel of wheat and a barrel of corn bought from the talkative cock — 'I don't care a damn, I will nyam and talk!' — and though the snake recaptures her once, the second barrelful buys the escape, and the snake beats the mother-in-law dead for it.
summary.zh: 歸途中，衣冠楚楚的求婚者須把領圈、外套一樣樣歸還，直到現出蛇身。他把新娘鎖起待誅，只待尋得『凸物』；岳母以成桶麥子玉米賄賂多嘴公雞——『管他呢，我邊吃邊唱！』——救出媳婦。蛇一度追回她，第二桶又換得脫身；蛇遂將岳母打死。

sensitivity.note: Animal-bridegroom variant. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: A woman had a daughter, oftentimes engaged and never married, saying the gentlemen were not to her sort — until one day she saw a well-dressed gentleman who came and proposed. She had a brother who was an Old Witch, and he told her that man was a snake; she said the man was too well-dressed to be a snake, but the brother went home with them under the carriage as a lizard. The first place, as he was going on, somebody asked, 'Mr. Snake, I beg you give me my collar' — then, 'Mr. Snake, I beg you give me my jacket' — and so on until he showed himself plain as a snake.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 86b (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: When they got home he locked her up, wanting to kill her, but could not kill her without the thing called 'bump', and went out in the yard looking for it. The mother-in-law said, 'Me daughter, the man you married is going to kill you, because he is a bad man and he married a wife already and killed her, and he is going to kill you too. I would let you go, but he has one cock, and he is so chat!' So she threw out a barrel of wheat and a barrel of corn, and when the cock was picking it up he said, 'I don't care a damn, I will nyam and talk!' — and sang, 'Ko ko re kom on do! Girl gone, him no gone...' The snake came from the wood while the brother was taking her on the water and overtook her, took her home again and locked her in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 86b, middle (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The mother-in-law threw out a double quantity of wheat and corn, and the cock ate all and sang again, 'Ko ko re kom on do! Girl gone, him no gone!' So when the snake came out from the wood he could not get her again, because she was near on land; he went back home and took a stick and licked the mother-in-law on the head and killed her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 86b, ending (2024/1924); not verbatim.

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (2024), tale 87 'Bull as Bridegroom' (a, Richard Morgan; b, George Parkes; c, Florence Thomlinson)

summary.en: The stout suitor who skips breakfast for clean grass is a bull in his off hours, going and coming on his own song. At the wedding feast the toast is refused in favor of the little brother's song — 'See me, Nancy, a wind; think a me, Nancy, me come' — and the groom's hair and four feet grow in, the big bull bucks down the wedding house and gallops out of the story forever. In the paired versions a knee that rings like a bell betrays the debbil when a child sings his own play-song under the table, and Miles the field-hand, overheard mooing his murder-intent, is roped and poled at the ball by the men his victim's little brother summons.
summary.zh: 不吃早飯卻去啃嫩草的壯漢，閒時原是公牛，進退皆循自譜之歌。婚宴上弟弟不受敬酒，改唱其歌——『南茜看我，如風而來』——新郎毛髮四蹄齊長，公牛撞塌婚宴、揚蹄絕塵而去。另一版本：會響鈴的膝蓋出賣魔鬼，孩子在他桌下唱他自己的戲歌；田間的邁爾斯哼唱殺機被弟弟聽破，舞會上被眾人繩套棒逐。

sensitivity.note: Animal-bridegroom exposure cycle. Collected from named tellers.

passages.text: There was a woman with a daughter. One day in the yard she saw a man, a big stout man, who put courtship to her and she said yes. When the man came to the yard at breakfast time he did not eat, but always went away where clean grass was; she had a brother watching him all the time. When he went, the man began to sing, 'See me, Nancy, a wind; think a me, Nancy, me come' — and the man turned bull and ate his belly full of grass. When he had eaten he sang again, 'See me, Nancy, a wind; think a me, Nancy, me gone' — and turned the shape of a man back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 87a (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the wedding day the boy said, 'Sister, do you know what that man coming here is? That man is a bull.' — 'O boy, go away! Where you ever hear a cow can turn a living soul?' They came home from church, sat round the table, everybody giving toast, and they called upon the woman's brother to give a toast. 'I won't give toast, but I will sing.' The guests said they would like to hear the sing as much as the toast, so the little boy commenced: 'See me, Nancy, a wind; think a me, Nancy, me come' — the man began to bawl out and knock his head, calling out for a toast; the boy sang again — the hair of the cow grew, and the four feet — and the big bull began to jump and buck down all the people in the house, and he galloped and they never saw him any more again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 87a, ending (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the paired version, the debbil dressed himself nicely to court a well-kept-up girl, and her witch-brother warned the mother he was the debbil — 'Go away, sah! what you know?' When the debbil walked, his knee sang like a ringing bell — 'Dirt i' room a yerry, double bing, double bing' — and if anybody else sang that song, the debbil's clothes dropped off, a horn grew on his head, and a tail grew out too. One night, while he talked in the house, the little boy underneath the table sang the song quietly; the debbil asked the mistress to stop the boy, who called it his little play-song — and the boy sang much louder, the debbil's knee sang very loud, the clothes dropped off and the tail and horns grew out. 'Didn't I tell you that man was a debbil, and you would not believe it!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 87b 'The Play-song' (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the third version, Miles courted Gracie and always sang for her — a song that Gracie was a fine girl but he was going to kill her — and she did not know he would kill her for true. Her little brother carried his breakfast to the field; before he got there Miles was not a man but a bull, turning man when he saw the boy coming. The boy told his sister, who called it nonsense until she followed and stayed far back and saw it was a bull eating grass, singing 'Me a Miles a moo, me Gracie is a fine girl, me Gracie me wi' kill her.' She raised a ball for the evening with men and ropes; when the little boy began the song, Miles demanded him turned out — but hoof and horn and tail began to grow, he got a big bull, and they tossed him and roped him and poled him and turned him out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 87c 'Gracie and Miles' (2024/1924); not verbatim.

title.en: Old Moody and Tep'y-tep'y: the Two Bulls
title.zh: 老穆迪與特比特比：雙牛記

source.work: Martha Warren Beckwith, 'Jamaica Anansi Stories' (2024 print) (2024), tale 88 'The Two Bulls' (told by Alexander Foster, Maroon Town)

summary.en: In Garshen pen the great bull Old Moody allows no bull-calf to live — but heifers he nurses and licks fine. A cow climbs a high mountain to drop a bull calf, and the mother waits till he is a tremendous bull, teaching him to test his father's tracks at the river. At last he will not wait: 'Ma, I gwine go see me father!' — and the two bulls sing challenge and answer across the common before the fight, the old one tossing the son into the air, and the son lifting the old one higher.
summary.zh: 加申牧場的老穆迪不容任何公牛犢存活——母牛犢卻被他舔育得膘肥體壯。一頭母牛攀上高山產下公犢；母親等他長成巨牛，教他在河邊試踩父親的蹄印。終於他不肯再等：『媽，我要去見我父親！』——兩頭公牛隔著牧場以歌相對、以角相迎：老的把兒子拋上半空，兒子落地四蹄穩立；兒子再把老的拋得更高。

sensitivity.note: Father-son combat tale ( patriarchal-succession type); collected from named tellers.

passages.text: One time there was a bull ranging the common — the pen called Garshen pen. That bull would not allow a bull-calf to be born and raised in that pen barring out his one self; but every heifer born he nursed, went about licking them, nourishing them, making them grow fine. Until one time a cow, heavy, climbed up into a high mountain and had a calf — and when the calf was born he was a bull calf. The old bull they called Old Moody, and the young bull 'Tep'y-tep'y-today'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 88 (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: The mother stayed until the calf grew a tremendous bull, and carried him down to the river to drink. Every time the father came to drink, he went away; when the son came, the son tried to put his foot in the father's track, and the bull mamma said to him, 'No, me son, the track no fit for you fader yet,' and carried him back a couple of days more. At twelve o'clock she carried him down again and he tried his foot for his father again — and now he felt to himself that he had become a man; he stood up in the same place and said, 'Must see me father today.' — 'Massy, me son, your pa is so cruel, there is a dread to carry son go!' He stood up and hollered, 'Ma, I gwine go! I gwine try to see me father!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 88, middle (2024/1924); not verbatim.

passages.text: He raised a song — 'Santy Moody o, Tep'y-tep'y deh!' — and the old bull answered, 'Hum-um-m, what you say? Me just a go a brudder Dickey an' Sandy; Moody say me mustn't go.' Coming up the common to meet his father, all the young girls turned out for that gentleman, and he sang coming — and the old bull answered again. They met to fight now, and the old one tossed his son up into the air and he dropped on four feet; and the son lifted him up in the air now...
passages.note: Paraphrase of Beckwith, tale 88, ending (2024/1924); not verbatim.
